c.tagline: Elegant City of Churches, with festivals, food, and famous wine at the doorstep.

taxi.fareNote: Fares are metered and a set surcharge applies to airport pickups; book by app or phone, or use ride-hail (Uber, Ola, DiDi).

emergency.note: 000 is Australia's national emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 112 also works from any mobile phone.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Hindley Street's late-night bar strip draws rowdy drunken crowds on weekends; keep usual awareness there after midnight.

hood_desc: Adelaide's compact grid heart, ringed by parklands and laced by a free tram line, packed with Rundle Mall shopping, the Central Market, museums, and the North Terrace cultural boulevard; best for first-timers who want everything within an easy walk.

A leafy, heritage district just across the River Torrens, full of bluestone cottages, historic pubs, and the cafe-and-restaurant strips of O'Connell and Melbourne Streets; suits travellers who want a calm, upscale base minutes from the CBD.

Adelaide's classic seaside suburb at the end of the tram line, built around the jetty, Moseley Square, and Glenelg Beach with its Jetty Road dining and sunsets over the Gulf St Vincent; ideal for a relaxed beach-town stay.

A cosmopolitan inner-eastern suburb centred on The Parade, a lively strip of boutiques, cafes, wine bars, and restaurants with a village feel; good for shoppers and diners who want local character away from the tourist core.

A regenerated former industrial pocket just northwest of the CBD, now a walkable, design-led urban village anchored by the Plant 4 food market and street art; suits younger travellers and creatives after a trendy, low-key scene.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some prefer filtered for taste.

transit.hours: Trains and the Glenelg tram run roughly 5am to midnight; the free City Connector buses run about 7am-7:15pm (to 9:15pm on Fridays). Late-night public transport is limited, so ride-hail fills the gap.
transit.pay: Tap on with a metroCARD (a A$5 reloadable smartcard) or the Buy & Go app; peak fares are about A$4.55 (~$3) and off-peak about A$2.60 (~$1.70), with a 2-hour transfer window. The free City Connector buses (routes 98 and 99) and the CBD tram free zone need no ticket at all.

transit.m: JetBus J1/J2 to the city (20-30 min)
Taxi to city centre (12-18 min, includes airport fee)

tip.r: Tipping is not expected in Australia; rounding up the bill or leaving around 10% for excellent service is appreciated but never required.

food.name: Pie floater
food.desc: An Adelaide oddity: a meat pie upended in a bowl of thick green pea soup, flooded with tomato sauce and eaten late at night.

places.name: Cafe de Vili's
places.note: Open around the clock and still serving the floater; the closest thing to the old pie-cart tradition.

places.name: Bakery on O'Connell
places.note: 24-hour bakery that keeps the late-night floater alive for taxi drivers and night owls.

places.name: Press Food and Wine
places.note: Modern Australian two-level room that puts a polished take on the floater on its menu.

food.name: King George whiting
food.desc: South Australia's most prized fish, sweet and delicate, usually grilled or lightly crumbed and served with chips and lemon.

places.name: Adelaide Central Market
places.note: Seafood stalls sell whiting fillets landed locally, and market eateries cook them to order.

places.name: Henley Beach Esplanade
places.note: Beachfront fish and chip shops where whiting is eaten from paper looking at the gulf.

places.name: Glenelg foreshore
places.note: Tram-ride seaside strip with a cluster of long-running seafood kitchens.

food.name: Coffin Bay oysters
food.desc: Eyre Peninsula oysters, plump and briny, shucked to order and eaten raw with nothing more than lemon or a splash of vinegar.

places.name: Adelaide Central Market
places.note: Market oyster bars shuck Coffin Bay and Smoky Bay oysters by the half dozen.

places.name: Adelaide Farmers Market
places.note: Sunday-morning market where SA growers and shuckers sell straight to the public.

food.name: Barossa and Adelaide Hills produce plate
food.desc: A grazing board of mettwurst and smallgoods from the Barossa's German settlers with Adelaide Hills cheeses, olives and local bread.

places.name: Barossa Fine Foods
places.note: Barossa smallgoods maker with a market counter; the mettwurst is the thing to buy.

places.name: Smelly Cheese Shop
places.note: Specialist cheesemonger stocking Adelaide Hills and Fleurieu producers, happy to build a board.

places.name: Adelaide Farmers Market
places.note: Direct-from-grower stalls for Hills cheese, charcuterie and bread on Sundays.

food.name: Frog cake
food.desc: A century-old Adelaide novelty: a sponge and cream cake iced into a green frog with its mouth wide open, declared a state heritage icon.

places.name: Balfours
places.area: Adelaide Central Market and CBD kiosks
places.note: The bakery that invented the frog cake in 1922 and still makes it.

places.name: Adelaide Central Market
places.note: Bakery stalls stock frog cakes alongside other South Australian sweets.

food.name: Haigh's chocolates
food.desc: Australia's oldest family chocolate maker, running in Adelaide since 1915; the chocolate frogs and rocky road are the local ritual buys.

places.name: Haigh's Beehive Corner
places.note: The landmark corner shop, trading since 1915 and a meeting point in its own right.

places.name: Haigh's Visitor Centre
places.note: Attached to the original factory, with free tastings and tours by booking.

food.name: Coopers ale
food.desc: Adelaide's family brewery since 1862, famous for bottle-conditioned Sparkling and Pale Ale; locals roll the bottle to stir the yeast.

places.name: Exeter Hotel
places.note: Scruffy, much-loved pub that is the standard Adelaide place for a Coopers Pale.

places.name: Wheatsheaf Hotel
places.note: Beer-focused local with an excellent tap list and courtyard, a fixture of the city's drinking scene.

places.name: Coopers Alehouse
places.note: Brewery-linked alehouse pouring the full range near the Regency Park brewery.

food.name: Barossa and Adelaide Hills wine
food.desc: Big Barossa shiraz, Clare riesling and cool-climate Hills chardonnay - four famous regions all sit within about an hour of the city.

places.name: National Wine Centre of Australia
places.area: Botanic Park, east of the CBD
places.note: Self-pour tasting wall of hundreds of Australian wines, strong on South Australian regions.

places.name: East End Cellars
places.note: Bottle shop and wine bar with deep Barossa and Hills lists and by-the-glass flights.

places.name: Adelaide Central Market
places.note: Market wine bars pour regional flights alongside the produce stalls.

landmarks: Adelaide Oval
A stunning riverside cricket and AFL stadium blending heritage grandstands with a striking modern design, offering some of the best skyline photo ops in the city.
St Peter's Cathedral
A soaring Gothic Revival Anglican cathedral with twin spires that has anchored North Adelaide's skyline since the 1870s.
Adelaide Central Market
One of the largest undercover produce markets in the Southern Hemisphere, bursting with colour, food stalls, and local culture.
Rundle Mall
Adelaide's premier pedestrian shopping strip, famous for the whimsical bronze 'Mall's Balls' sculpture that's a favourite photo spot.
Adelaide Botanic Garden
A lush 19th-century botanic garden featuring a giant Amazon waterlily pavilion, rose gardens, and a striking bicentennial conservatory.
Mount Lofty Summit
The highest point in the Adelaide Hills, delivering panoramic views over the entire city and coastline, especially magical at sunset.
Glenelg Beach
A postcard-perfect stretch of sand with a historic jetty, palm-lined promenade, and vintage tram connecting it to the city.
Art Gallery of South Australia
A grand sandstone gallery on North Terrace housing one of Australia's finest art collections in an elegant heritage building.
Adelaide Festival Centre
A bold Brutalist-modernist arts complex on the banks of the Torrens River, the heart of Adelaide's cultural and festival scene.
Parliament House, Adelaide
An imposing marble-columned neoclassical building on North Terrace that is a striking symbol of South Australian democracy.

train.note: Australia has no international trains. From Adelaide, Journey Beyond runs three iconic long-distance services (journeybeyondrail.com.au): The Overland to Melbourne (a full-day daytime run), The Ghan north through the Outback to Alice Springs and Darwin, and the Indian Pacific east to Sydney and west to Perth. These are premium, infrequent experiences rather than everyday transport; commuter trains only serve Adelaide's suburbs.

bus.note: No international coaches, as Australia is an island continent. Long-distance coaches leave from the Adelaide Central Bus Station on Franklin Street: Firefly Express (fireflyexpress.com.au) runs overnight Adelaide-Melbourne-Sydney services, and operators such as Premier Stateliner and LinkSA connect regional South Australia.

ferry.note: No scheduled international or city passenger ferries. The nearest sea link is SeaLink's vehicle-and-passenger ferry to Kangaroo Island, which sails from Cape Jervis about 100km south of the city rather than from Adelaide itself.

half.name: Adelaide Hills & Hahndorf
half.blurb: A cool-climate escape of rolling vineyards, cellar doors, and Hahndorf, Australia's oldest surviving German settlement, with its Bavarian pubs and craft shops.

half.name: McLaren Vale
half.blurb: A relaxed coastal wine region 45 minutes south, famous for bold Shiraz, olive groves, and long lunches at architecturally striking cellar doors like d'Arenberg.

half.name: Mount Lofty & Cleland
half.blurb: The summit lookout over the whole city and gulf, paired with Cleland Wildlife Park where you can meet koalas and kangaroos up close.

half.name: Port Adelaide
half.blurb: The historic maritime quarter with heritage warehouses, museums, weekend markets, and dolphin-spotting cruises along the Port River.

full.name: Barossa Valley
full.blurb: One of the world's great wine regions, an hour northeast, dense with landmark wineries such as Penfolds, Seppeltsfield, and Jacob's Creek plus artisan food producers.

full.name: Kangaroo Island
full.blurb: A wildlife-rich island of sea-lion colonies, wind-sculpted rock formations, and untouched beaches, reached by ferry from Cape Jervis for a big but rewarding day.

full.name: Victor Harbor & Fleurieu Peninsula
full.blurb: A seaside town where a horse-drawn tram crosses to Granite Island; the surrounding Fleurieu coast offers whale watching in winter and clifftop drives.

full.name: Clare Valley
full.blurb: A quieter northern wine valley celebrated for world-class Riesling, historic stone villages, and the Riesling Trail cycling path between cellar doors.
